title: Electromagnetic field theories of conscious experience: a conceptual review and reappraisal
titleZh: 意识体验的电磁场理论：概念回顾与重新评价
abstract: Abstract This paper reviews and contrasts electromagnetic field (EMF) theories of consciousness with traditional neural and functionalist accounts of phenomenal space and its contents. Conscious experience is unified yet differentiated, intentional, reportable, and capable of influencing behaviour. These properties, available only from a first-person perspective, must correspond to distinct states or processes in an underlying physical substrate. Conventional neural and functionalist theories explain conscious experience through local causal interactions among discrete units and symbolic processing. However, patterns of computation and causal organization exist only from an external observer’s perspective and therefore do not themselves explain subjective experience. In contrast, the brain’s endogenous EMF, which integrates information spatially, provides a plausible substrate for phenomenal unity. Evidence linking EMF dynamics to conscious states and contents is abundant, particularly from EEG studies showing reliable correlations despite attenuation of extracranial fields. EMF dynamics may also provide a more stable representation of short-term memory than variable neural firing patterns. Evidence for ephaptic coupling further demonstrates that EMFs influence neural activity, potentially contributing to rapid large-scale neural coordination and fluctuations in firing thresholds. Experimental perturbation of endogenous EMFs can alter conscious experience and modulate oscillations involved in memory consolidation. EMFs can perform field computation through superposition, and a gradual evolutionary origin follows from the adaptive advantages of ephaptic coupling in simpler nervous systems. It is hypothesized that low-frequency oscillations provide the basis of phenomenal space, whereas localized high-frequency oscillations support experiential differentiation. Intentionality is explained by locating the conscious EMF between sensory input and motor output processes.
